Case study: age-associated cell types across eight cohorts

Source: vignettes/stablr-aging-case-study.Rmd
stablr-aging-case-study.Rmd

Summary. We apply the stablr environment-stability workflow to a public aging atlas. The atlas has 2,609 donors from eight scRNA-seq cohorts. The workflow finds 24 of 60 features that track age in every cohort. This full-atlas selection is exploratory. Per-cohort knockoff diagnostics (FDP+) are close to 1 on this atlas. The selection bar is therefore a descriptive reproducibility filter, not calibrated error control. Seven of eight age-associated cell types from the source publication pass the selection bar. All eight keep the same direction of effect in all cohorts. Models trained on seven cohorts predict age in the eighth cohort. The all-feature model reaches a mean absolute error of 6.7 to 15.6 years, depending on the held-out cohort. The selected-panel model uses features chosen with all eight cohorts. Its error is a post-selection estimate, not complete-pipeline held-out validation. A selection-isolated LOCO that re-selects inside each training partition gives a pooled error of 12.3 years. This vignette is an application case study. It is not calibration evidence for the method.

Status of this vignette (2026-10-15). This vignette is the historical exploratory analysis (v1). A prospective revision with a locked protocol, a leakage-proof engine, a six-selector matrix, and a permutation null has since been completed (v2). Section 10 summarizes the v2 design and findings; the v2 package lives in benchmarks/ws8_v2/. Three v1 defects found by audit are flagged where they occur: the exported mean_score and selected_lasso columns are entirely missing (so the lasso sensitivity claim is not verifiable from the committed table), and the script-level and vignette-level MAE summaries used different estimands (micro vs macro). The v1 numbers below are otherwise as committed. Where v1 and v2 differ, v2 is authoritative. A v3 candidate benchmark (2026-10-21, benchmarks/ws8_v3/) then extended the six-selector matrix with four candidate mechanisms and ComBat baselines on a pinned package; Section 10.9 summarizes its findings and the resulting division of labor between the environment-stability workflow and meta-analytic ranking.

1 Background and aims

A biomarker panel must work in new cohorts. A feature can track age in one cohort and fail in the next. Cohort differences in cell composition can cause this failure. Differences in sample processing can cause it too. Chance can also cause it.

The environment-stability workflow in stablr fits the selection procedure in each cohort separately. It then keeps only the features that pass the selection bar in all cohorts.

This case study asks two questions:

  1. Which cell-type features track age in the same direction in all eight cohorts?
  2. Do the selected features predict age in a cohort that the model did not see?

The analysis ran once with a fixed seed. The analysis script is benchmarks/ws8_aging_showcase.R in the package source. The figures and statistics tables come from benchmarks/ws8_figures.R and benchmarks/ws8_recalibration.R. The pipeline takes about 15 minutes. The post-review follow-up analyses add about one hour, most of it the selection-isolated LOCO. This vignette shows the saved results.

2 Data

2.1 Source and availability

The data come from a public healthy-aging PBMC atlas (Terekhova et al. 2026, Immunity). The Artyomov lab single-cell portal distributes the atlas (dataset pan_atlas_healthy_aging_all_celtypes). We downloaded the per-cell annotation table all_cells_metadata.csv.gz on 2026-10-13. The file has 13,137,775 cells (MD5 50651968855bf6ca3efcdf199e2a9fd5). Each row is one cell. The columns include donor id, age, sex, CMV status, ancestry, cohort, and cell-type annotation.

2.2 Cohorts

Cohort Donors
OneK1K 981
AIDA 625
CIMA 421
KCL 188
ABF300 166
UCSF 99
SoundLife 96
SPAC 33
Total 2609

The cohorts differ in size, ancestry mix, and age range. Cohort identity explains the largest share of variance in the atlas (Terekhova et al. 2026). This property makes the atlas a strong test for transportability.

2.3 Donor-level feature construction

Each donor is one sample. For each donor and each cell type, we compute a smoothed proportion: (count + 0.5) / (total + 0.5). We then apply the logit transform. This gives 59 cell-type features. One covariate (sex, coded Female = 1) joins the panel.

Three covariate columns are constant inside at least one cohort: CMV status and two ancestry indicators. The analysis drops them. A constant column has no within-cohort signal. Its zero variance also breaks the equicorrelated knockoff construction. No cell-type feature is constant in any cohort.

The final panel has 60 features. The outcome is donor age in years. The environments are the eight cohorts.

The donor-level count table was derived from the per-cell annotation table before the analysis script runs. That derivation script is not part of the package source. The predesign predeclares excluding cells flagged Bad quality. This vignette cannot verify that step.

3 Statistical methods

3.1 Selection procedure

This section uses four defined terms:

  • Selection frequency: how often a feature is selected across 200 bootstrap resamples of one cohort.
  • Decoy feature: a knockoff artificial feature. It carries no signal. A real feature must beat the decoys to be selected.
  • Min-agg score: the minimum selection frequency of a feature across the eight cohorts.
  • Consistent feature: a feature with a min-agg score of at least 0.5.

For each cohort separately, stabl_environment_stability() runs the STABL procedure (Hédou et al. 2024) with these settings:

  • Base learner: random forest (ranger, 500 trees, permutation importance).
  • Decoys: model-X equicorrelated knockoff features, injected at a 1:1 ratio.
  • Resampling: 200 bootstrap resamples, classic bootstrap design (sample_fraction = 1, replace = TRUE).
  • Seed: 20261013.

The min-agg rule follows the aggregation of the WS-5 simulation study. That study measured FDP+ between 0.083 and 0.142 across shift and drift designs. Section 4.1 reports the FDP+ diagnostics of this atlas. They do not reproduce the WS-5 calibration here. See ?stabl_environment_stability.

3.2 Uncertainty and sign consistency

The selection frequency is a binomial proportion over 200 resamples. For each feature, we report the exact 95% Clopper–Pearson interval of the weakest cohort. The weakest cohort sets the min-agg score. The interval covers one binomial proportion. It does not account for the min-agg rule taking the minimum over eight cohorts.

We also test the direction of each feature with an exact sign test. A feature with the same correlation sign in 8 of 8 cohorts has p = 0.0078. The sign test assumes between-cohort independence.

3.3 Sensitivity analysis

The primary analysis uses the random-forest learner. The WS-2 simulation calibrated this learner for gaussian problems with up to a few dozen predictors (mean FDP+ 0.025 linear, 0.065 nonlinear). Select it with base_learner = "rf".

As a sensitivity analysis, we repeat the full workflow with the lasso learner. The knockoff type, the bootstrap count, and the seed stay the same. The lasso can be anti-conservative in some regimes (WS-2: FDP+ 0.58 at p = 50). We read the lasso result as a direction check only.

3.4 Age prediction

We use leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) evaluation. Each fold trains a ridge model (glmnet, alpha = 0, 5-fold internal CV) on seven cohorts. The fold then predicts donor age in the eighth cohort. We evaluate two models: ridge on all 60 features, and ridge on the 24 consistent features.

The two models answer different questions. The all-feature model is a genuine held-out evaluation: the held-out cohort plays no role in the feature set or the fit. The selected-panel model is different. The 24 features were chosen with all eight cohorts, including the held-out one. Its LOCO error is therefore a post-selection estimate. It is apparent for the selection procedure, not an unbiased held-out error for the full workflow. Section 5.1 reports a selection-isolated LOCO, which re-selects features inside each seven-cohort training partition.

We report three quantities per held-out cohort:

  • Mean absolute error (MAE) with 95% bootstrap intervals. The intervals use 2,000 donor-level resamples inside the held-out cohort.
  • Calibration slope. This slope comes from a linear fit of predicted age on observed age. This is the inverse of the usual observed-on-predicted calibration regression. The two agree only at perfect calibration. A slope of 1 is ideal. A slope below 1 means the predictions shrink toward the middle of the age range.
  • Pearson correlation between predicted and observed age.

4 Result: features that track age in every cohort

The min-agg rule selects 24 of the 60 features. Figure 1 ranks all features by min-agg score. The grey whiskers show the exact 95% interval of the weakest cohort. The dashed line is the 0.5 bar. Crosses mark the eight features that the source publication predeclared as age-associated.

Minimum cross-cohort selection frequency (min-agg score) for all 60 features. Blue bars pass the 0.5 bar; grey bars do not. Grey whiskers show the exact 95% Clopper–Pearson interval of the weakest cohort. Crosses mark the eight predeclared features.

4.1 The selection bar is not FDR-controlled on this atlas

Each per-cohort fit carries its own knockoff decoys, so each fit has an FDP+ diagnostic. The predesign asked for these diagnostics as success criterion 2. They were computed inside every fit but not reported. Table 1 reports them. The result is adverse.

Table 1: Per-environment FDP+ diagnostics (rf + knockoff_equi, 200 bootstraps). “FDP+ at 0.5 bar” evaluates the diagnostic at the threshold of the min-agg rule. The last two columns count features whose maximum-over-lambda score passes 0.5.

Cohort n Min FDP+ (threshold) FDP+ at 0.5 bar Real ≥ 0.5 Decoys ≥ 0.5
ABF300 166 1.00 (0.99) 1.03 59 60
AIDA 625 1.00 (0.98) 1.03 59 60
CIMA 421 0.92 (0.85) 1.03 59 60
KCL 188 0.94 (0.85) 1.05 40 42
OneK1K 981 1.02 (1.00) 1.03 59 60
SoundLife 96 0.89 (0.93) 1.04 56 57
SPAC 33 0.95 (0.77) 1.03 36 38
UCSF 99 0.89 (0.55) 1.04 48 51

In every cohort, decoy features pass the 0.5 bar as often as real features. Even the best threshold per cohort leaves FDP+ between 0.89 and 1.02. The WS-5 calibration (0.083 to 0.142) does not transfer to this atlas. Plausible causes include the compositional feature space, the max-over-lambda score, and cohorts with fewer donors than features. This case study does not pick a cause.

The reading changes accordingly. On this atlas, the min-agg rule is a descriptive reproducibility filter. It is not calibrated FDR control. The evidence for the selected panel is the sign consistency below, the agreement with the predeclared features, and the held-out prediction results. It is not the knockoff calibration.

Table 2 lists the eight predeclared features. Seven of eight pass the bar. The near-miss is CD8+ Tem GZMB+ with a score of 0.445. Its interval includes 0.5. The data cannot separate it from the bar. The predeclared rule does not select it.

All eight directions agree with the source publication. The naive and recent-thymic-emigrant compartments fall with age. MAIT falls with age. The terminal-effector compartments rise with age.

Figure 2 shows the per-cohort Spearman correlation for the 24 consistent features. Three observations matter:

  1. The top rows are sign-consistent and moderately strong in all cohorts. These rows are CD8+ T Naive, CD8+ RTE, CD4+ RTE, and MAIT.
  2. Only 11 of the 24 consistent features reach sign-test significance at 0.05 (uncorrected; 24 tests). The panel has a strongly replicable core and a weaker periphery.
  3. SPAC (n = 33) flips the sign of several weak features. Small cohorts dominate the sign pattern of weak rows.
Per-cohort Spearman correlation with age for the 24 consistent features, ordered by mean correlation. Orange is negative. Blue is positive.

The lasso sensitivity analysis selects 6 features under the same rule. CD8+ T Naive is the only feature that both learners select. The agreement is partial. The lasso result supports the direction of the primary result. It does not reproduce the full 24-feature panel.

Audit note (v2): the exported selected_lasso column is missing for all 60 features in the committed results table (a name-stripping defect in the export). The “6 features” count above is therefore not verifiable from the committed artifact; treat it as a narrative claim from the run log. The v2 revision replaces this sensitivity with a matched-budget lasso stability comparator (selector M2, Section 10).

4.2 Which cohort sets the bar

The min-agg score is a minimum over cohorts. For all 24 selected features, that minimum is set by one of the five smallest cohorts. SPAC (n = 33) sets it for 10 of 24 features (12 of 24 if ties count; two features have a selection frequency of 1.000 in all eight cohorts). UCSF (n = 99) sets it for 7, KCL (n = 188) for 4, ABF300 (n = 166) for 2, and SoundLife (n = 96) for 1. No minimum is set by one of the three large cohorts.

SPAC is the weakest link. It has fewer donors than features (33 < 60). The equicorrelated knockoff covariance is therefore a positive-definite projection of a rank-deficient sample covariance. A bootstrap resample of 33 donors contains about 21 unique donors. The claim that a feature “tracks age in every cohort” is limited by SPAC for 10 of the 24 features.

4.3 Sensitivity: min-agg without SPAC

We repeat the min-agg rule over the seven cohorts without SPAC. The panel grows from 24 to 33 features. Nine features join; none leave. The predeclared set keeps its status: CD8+ Tem GZMK+ rises from 0.505 to 0.660; the other seven scores do not change. Given the FDP+ result above, neither panel size is calibrated. The sensitivity shows that panel membership depends on the smallest cohort. It does not show that the larger panel is better.

5 Result: age prediction on held-out cohorts

Table 3 and Figure 3 give the LOCO results. Read the two columns as different estimands. The all-feature column is a genuine held-out evaluation. The selected column is a post-selection estimate, because the 24 features were chosen with all eight cohorts. The all-feature model predicts age with MAE between 6.7 years (SoundLife) and 15.6 years (CIMA). The selected-feature model helps two cohorts clearly: CIMA (15.6 to 7.6 years) and UCSF (13.4 to 10.8 years). It hurts two others: OneK1K (15.5 to 17.7 years) and SoundLife (6.7 to 9.6 years). The overall means (12.1 and 11.7 years) hide this heterogeneity.

Audit note (v2): the means quoted here are macro means (unweighted over cohorts). The analysis script’s own pooled summary was a micro mean (donor-weighted, 14.0 years for the all-feature model). The two estimands were presented under one name in v1; v2 reports both, explicitly labeled (Section 10).

A paired per-donor comparison makes this precise (Table 4). For each donor, we take the difference of absolute errors (all-feature minus selected; positive favors the panel). The improvement is 8.0 years [7.3, 8.7] in CIMA and 2.6 [1.9, 3.3] in UCSF. The loss is 2.2 [−2.5, −1.9] in OneK1K and 2.8 [−3.9, −1.6] in SoundLife. ABF300, KCL, and SPAC show no clear difference. Pooled over all donors, the panel improves the MAE by 0.5 years [0.3, 0.7]. The paired intervals resolve the overlap of the marginal intervals in Table 3: the UCSF improvement is real. One caveat: the two models differ in covariates. The all-feature model includes sex; the selected panel does not (sex was not selected). The paired comparison mixes a change of feature set with a change of covariate set.

Figure 4 shows predicted versus observed age for the selected-feature model. The correlation is between 0.58 and 0.78 (r² between 0.34 and 0.61). Every calibration slope is below 1 (0.30 to 0.75). The predictions shrink toward the training range in all cohorts. OneK1K shrinks most (slope 0.30). KCL and SoundLife shrink least (0.71 to 0.75).

The source publication reports 8.2 years test MAE for its trained clock. Our protocol is simpler and different: a ridge model on donor-level proportions, trained on seven cohorts and applied to the eighth. The two numbers are not directly comparable. The honest reading is this. Composition features carry cross-cohort age signal. The ranking quality is good. The calibration loss is cohort-specific.

LOCO predicted versus observed age for the selected-feature model, one panel per held-out cohort. The dashed line is the identity line. Annotations give the donor count, the calibration slope, and the Pearson r.

5.1 Selection-isolated LOCO

The selected-panel column above is a post-selection estimate. A selection-isolated LOCO removes the selection leakage. The protocol is predeclared in the predesign addendum 2. Inside each seven-cohort training partition, we rerun the full selection (rf + knockoff_equi, 200 bootstraps, min-agg at 0.5 over the seven training cohorts) and predict the eighth cohort with the within-fold panel.

Table 5: Selection-isolated LOCO. “Panel” is the within-fold panel size. “Overlap” counts how many of the 24 full-data panel features the fold re-selects. The last two columns repeat Table 3.

Cohort n Panel Overlap MAE selection-isolated (95% CI) MAE all MAE post-selection

Three readings matter.

  1. The pooled complete-pipeline error is 12.3 years. The post-selection mean (11.7) was mildly optimistic, as expected. The all-feature mean (12.1) is close to the complete-pipeline value.
  2. The CIMA improvement does not survive selection isolation. The within-fold panel has 41 features and predicts CIMA with 17.0 years, worse than the all-feature model (15.6). The improvement in Table 3 (15.6 to 7.6) is specific to the fixed full-data panel. It is a property of that panel, not of the workflow.
  3. The UCSF improvement survives (13.4 to 11.0). The panel core is stable: every fold re-selects at least 22 of the 24 full-data features. The same two features (CD4+ Treg naive, CD8+ Temra) drop in seven of eight folds.

6 Result: per-cohort recalibration

The slope gap raises a practical question. Can a per-cohort recalibration map fix the compression? We tested this question with a nested design. This section recalibrates the selected-panel predictions. These are a post-selection estimand (Section 5). The recalibration numbers inherit that label. Inside each held-out cohort, we cross-validated the recalibration map itself (5 folds, 5 repeats). We compared two maps: a linear map and an isotonic (monotone) map. All evaluation is out-of-fold.

Recalibration helps where compression dominates. In OneK1K, linear recalibration halves the selected-panel MAE: from 17.7 to 9.8 years (post-selection numbers; the all-feature MAE is 15.5). Isotonic gives 9.6 years. AIDA improves from 14.1 to 8.1 years. UCSF improves from 10.8 to 7.0 years. ABF300 does not improve (9.4 to 9.3 years). Its error was already scatter, not compression. SPAC gets worse (14.3 to 14.9 years). A cohort of 33 donors cannot support a recalibration map.

The slope gap does not close fully. After linear recalibration, the out-of-fold slope moves from 0.30 to 0.45 in OneK1K. This value equals the squared correlation (r² = 0.454). The same identity holds in all eight cohorts. The largest deviation is 0.02. Figure 5 shows this identity: the after-recalibration points sit on the r² markers.

The identity has a clear meaning. Recalibration removes the systematic compression. It cannot remove noise. The remaining slope gap is the share of variance that the predictions do not explain.

Calibration slope of LOCO predictions before and after cross-validated linear recalibration. The orange diamonds mark the r-squared identity: the expected out-of-fold slope after recalibration.

7 Discussion

Three findings generalize beyond this atlas.

First, the strongly replicable core is small. Three features have a selection frequency of at least 0.99 in every cohort: CD8+ T Naive, CD8+ RTE, and CD4+ RTE. Two more clear 0.8: CD4+ T HLA-DR+ memory (0.82) and CD8+ IFN+ cells (0.81). The predeclared CD4+ Temra (0.755) and MAIT (0.740) pass the bar, but their selection frequency is not near 1. The near-1 core matches the biology of the source publication. Thymic involution and T-cell compartment restructuring are the most reproducible immune-aging signatures.

Second, selection frequency and effect size are different quantities. The min-agg bar asks for replicable selection. It does not ask for a large or sign-stable correlation. Eleven of the 24 consistent features have weak or cohort-mixed correlations. A direct comparison makes this concrete. Only 13 of the 24 consistent features also pass a significance vote (significant in at least 5 of 8 cohorts, BH-adjusted). Eight other features pass that vote but fail min-agg. The two rules select different feature types. A reader who needs a compact panel can take the replicable core. A reader who needs the full panel must treat the periphery as hypotheses.

Third, prediction quality is cohort-specific. The paired per-donor differences (Section 5) confirm the pattern: the selected panel improves CIMA by 8.0 years and UCSF by 2.6, and worsens OneK1K by 2.2 and SoundLife by 2.8. The selection-isolated LOCO tempers the CIMA result: that improvement is specific to the fixed full-data panel and does not survive complete-pipeline isolation (Section 5.1). Cohort identity is the largest variance component of the atlas. No composition-only model will calibrate uniformly across such cohorts. The LOCO design makes this cost visible. A pooled metric would hide it.

8 Limits

Four limits bound the conclusions.

  1. Application case study, not calibration evidence. The calibration evidence for the random-forest learner is simulation-based (WS-2). That evidence covers gaussian problems with up to a few dozen predictors. This panel has 60 features. The showcase demonstrates the workflow on real data. It does not add calibration guarantees. On this atlas, the per-cohort FDP+ diagnostics are close to 1 (Section 4.1). The selection bar is a descriptive filter here.
  2. Selected-panel LOCO is post-selection. The 24 consistent features were chosen with all eight cohorts. The selected-panel LOCO error is therefore apparent for the selection procedure, not an unbiased held-out error for the full workflow. The all-feature LOCO column is the genuine held-out evaluation here. A selection-isolated LOCO that re-selects features inside each training partition is reported in Section 5.1.
  3. The min-agg rule is conservative by design. A feature must pass the bar in every cohort. Features with cohort-specific signal fail the bar. Their biology can still be real. CD8+ Tem GZMB+ (score 0.445) is the predeclared example. The min-agg score is set by the smallest cohorts for all 24 features (Section 4.2).
  4. Composition features are relative. Logit proportions measure a cell type against all typed cells. An increase in one compartment mechanically dilutes the others. The direction claims are about composition. They are not about absolute abundance.
  5. Single run. The analysis uses one seed (20261013). The bootstrap intervals quantify sampling noise inside that run. They do not cover seed-level variation of the full pipeline.

10 The v2 prospective revision

10.1 Why a revision

The v1 analysis above was exploratory. A later audit found export defects and an estimand conflation (flagged in place above), and the design mixed selection and evaluation on the same cohorts. The v2 revision rebuilds the case study as a prospective benchmark with a locked protocol (benchmarks/ws8_v2/protocol.md), a leakage-proof leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) engine, six matched selectors, and a permutation null. Every v2 claim traces to a committed, executed artifact in the claims ledger (claims_ledger.md). An independent adversarial review of the v2 package was performed and all findings were remediated (review_decisions.md, Amendment 1 in ws8_showcase_predesign.md).

10.2 Design in brief

The feature universe is the 59 harmonized immune cell-type proportions (sex, CMV, and ancestry are not discovery features). Each of the eight cohorts is held out in turn. Selectors train on the remaining seven cohorts only: M0, a random-effects meta-analysis of per-cohort associations; M1, the source paper’s per-cohort adjusted significance vote (feature ~ age + sex + ancestry, BH, at least 5 of 7 cohorts); M2, pooled lasso stability; M3, pooled STABL; M4, environment-aware STABL with min-across-cohorts aggregation (the primary method); M5, the same with majority aggregation. The primary endpoint is the cohort-balanced held-out directional replication R(K): the mean, over the matched top-K panel (K = 10), of the training-signed held-out Spearman correlation with age, averaged over the eight folds. The confirmatory contrasts are M4 versus M0 and M4 versus M3. M3 is the controlled pair for M4: identical learner, knockoffs, budget, and seed; only the cohort aggregation differs.

10.3 Result: held-out association replication

Macro R at K = 10 across the eight held-out cohorts:

Selector Macro R@10
M0 meta-analysis 0.395
M1 adjusted vote 0.386
M5 env STABL, majority 0.321
M4 env STABL, min 0.286
M3 pooled STABL 0.142
M2 lasso stability 0.118
Per-cohort held-out signed replication at K = 10 for the six selectors. Diamonds are macro means.

The confirmatory contrasts (paired over the eight cohorts; intervals are paired t intervals on 7 degrees of freedom, imprecise at n = 8; p-values are exact sign-flip tests):

  • M4 − M3 = +0.145 [+0.083, +0.206], p = 0.0078. Environment-aware aggregation adds value over pooled STABL. The difference is positive in all eight cohorts. This is the controlled isolation of the aggregation step.
  • M4 − M0 = −0.108 [−0.174, −0.043], p = 0.016. The min-aggregated STABL panel replicates less well than the simple random-effects meta-analysis ranking.

Exploratory contrasts: M4 − M1 = −0.100 (p = 0.023), M4 − M2 = +0.168 (p = 0.0078), M4 − M5 = −0.034 (p = 0.023). The reading is mixed and partly negative for the primary hypothesis. Environment-aware aggregation beats pooling the cohorts into one STABL fit, and beats lasso stability. It does not beat the simpler association-based selectors — the meta-analysis or the significance vote — at the same feature budget. No method-superiority claim is made.

A post-merge re-aggregation probe (S2b, 2026-10-16) re-scores the persisted M4 environment selections at cohort-count quantiles instead of the minimum. A 25% quantile (M4q25) reaches macro R@10 0.362 — above both M4 (0.287; paired difference +0.076 [+0.025, +0.127], sign-flip p = 0.023) and M5 (0.321) — while a 10% quantile does not (−0.006, NS). The predeclared falsification hook fired: strict-min aggregation is suboptimal on this atlas, not merely conservative. The probe re-uses the persisted M4 scores without refitting (the q = 0 control reproduces the committed M4 values to 5e-16); it is exploratory and single-atlas (claims ledger V5, upgraded).

10.4 Result: the selection count is null-saturated

The S0 null probe permutes age within each cohort (preserving the features, the cohort structure, and each cohort’s age distribution) and refits the full M4 selector. In 50 of 50 permutations, the min-aggregation rule selects 59 of 59 features at the 0.5 bar (Clopper–Pearson 95% lower bound for the saturation probability: 0.929). The same-design real-data fit selects 35 of 59. Under the null, the selector selects everything; the size of the selected panel therefore carries no signal on this atlas. This is consistent with the v1 knockoff diagnostics (FDP+ close to 1, Section 4.1). Every per-environment fit containing SPAC (n = 33 donors, fewer than the 59 features) uses a positive-definite projection of a rank-deficient knockoff covariance, and min-aggregation gives that smallest cohort veto power; the saturation and the projection were plausibly related as this section first went to press. A SPAC-excluded rerun of the full null probe (50 permutations, seven cohorts; Section 10.8) saturates identically — 50/50 permutations select 59/59 (Clopper–Pearson lower bound 0.942) against 30/59 native on the SPAC-excluded real-data fit — so the projection is not the mechanism, and synthetic simulations reproduce the saturation under every truth regime including the null. The v2 case for the panel rests on the replication and prediction rankings above and below — not on selection being non-null.

Features selected by the M4 min-aggregation rule under 50 within-cohort age permutations (points) versus the same-design real-data fit (dashed line, 35 of 59).

10.5 Result: prediction in unseen cohorts

A ridge model on the M4 top-10 panel, tuned by leave-one-training-cohort-out inner CV, predicts held-out cohort age with macro MAE 12.2 years (micro 13.6), against 12.4 (14.4) for the all-59 model and 20.1 (22.7) for the training-median baseline. The panel beats the median baseline decisively (paired per-cohort difference −7.9 years [−11.1, −4.7], sign-flip p = 0.0078). It does not beat the all-59 model systematically (−0.16 years [−2.84, +2.51], p = 0.93); the macro edge rests on one cohort (CIMA), and the top-10 panel is worse than all-59 in five of eight cohorts. Calibration slopes remain below 1 in every cohort (predicted-on- observed 0.32 to 0.68): predictions compress toward the training range, as in v1 Section 5.

10.6 Result: biology

All eight a priori reference populations keep the same direction of association in all eight cohorts: naive and recent-thymic-emigrant T cells and MAIT cells fall with age; terminally differentiated effector-memory compartments rise. The GZMK+/GZMB+ CD8 effector-memory ratio is cohort-dependent (negative in six of eight cohorts): a reproducible core coexists with cohort-dependent components. Per-cohort effect sizes and heterogeneity are in benchmarks/ws8_v2/results/biology/.

10.7 What v2 changes

The v1 headline — 24 of 60 features “track age in every cohort” — survives only in a weaker, audited form. The selection bar is not non-null on this atlas (Section 10.4), so panel membership itself is not evidence. What survives is the ranking: the strongest age-associated features replicate in held-out cohorts under every selector, the eight predeclared populations are directionally consistent everywhere, and a sparse panel predicts age in unseen cohorts about as well as the full feature set. For this endpoint on this atlas, the simplest selectors (meta-analysis or a significance vote) replicate best; environment-aware STABL’s measured value is its improvement over pooled STABL, not superiority over simpler baselines.

10.8 Post-merge robustness and calibration follow-ups

Four predeclared follow-ups (2026-10-16) probe the v2 findings; the claims ledger carries the full entries (V11–V15).

  • SPAC exclusion (S2a). Re-running the six-selector LOCO on the seven cohorts without SPAC preserves the ordering (M0 0.408 > M1 0.395 > M5 0.344 > M4 0.323 > M3 0.190 > M2 0.141) and the confirmatory M4 − M3 contrast (+0.133 [+0.069, +0.197], p = 0.016). The headline is robust to the one cohort whose knockoff covariance needed projection.
  • Aggregation quantile (S2b). Reported with Section 10.3: a 25% quantile aggregation beats both min and majority; the V5 status is upgraded from tentative to supported.
  • Knockoff construction (S2c). Replacing knockoff_equi with knockoff_mvr moves the M4 macro R@10 by −0.002 (0.284 vs 0.286); the findings are not an artifact of the equi construction.
  • Synthetic calibration (S1). A simulator anchored to the real per-cohort means, pooled covariance, and empirical ages runs four truth regimes (homogeneous, heterogeneous, null, sparse-strong) through the same six selectors. M4 and M5 select every native feature under all four — including the pure null — with empirical FDP 0.83–1.00: the saturation is structural, not an atlas property. Under known truth, per-cohort STABL voting (M1) matches the association ranking under homogeneity (R@10 0.203 vs 0.203), nominally exceeds it under heterogeneity (0.160 vs 0.154), selects nothing under the null, and recovers exactly the sparse truth (top-10 recovery 1.00, sign accuracy 1.00, native FDP 0). The full calibration runs 20 replicates per scenario (80 total; inputs, seeds, and per-replicate results are committed; benchmarks/ws8_v2/results/s1/). Under the pure null every arm sits at noise level (|R@10| ≤ 0.005). Reps 1–5 predate the v3 package pin and reps 6–20 ran on the pinned commit; the pooled conclusions match the pilot, so the ranking story is not sensitive to the version drift.

10.9 The v3 candidate benchmark (2026-10-21)

A third revision (benchmarks/ws8_v3/, branch ws8-v3-candidates) kept the v2 protocol (8-fold leave-one-cohort-out, macro R@10 primary endpoint, seed 20261013) and pinned the package at one commit (a8f3a58) to remove the version drift between v2-era runs. It re-ran M0–M5 like-for-like and added four candidate mechanisms plus ComBat baselines: M6, a heterogeneity-filtered random-effects meta-analysis; M7, MINT-STABL (integrative multi-cohort selection) with a tuned control M7c; M8, contrast-penalized STABL; and M9, ComBat-merge-then-select, with transform controls M9b/M9s.

Findings that update this vignette:

  • The M4 − M0 contrast replicates on the pinned package, attenuated. Like-for-like macro R@10: M0 0.395, M1 0.386, M5 0.354, M4 0.327, M3 0.142, M2 0.118. M0–M3 reproduce bit-exactly; the environment-stability wrapper itself changed between the v2-era commits and the pin, moving M4 from 0.286 to 0.327 and M5 from 0.321 to 0.354. M4 − M0 = −0.068 [−0.122, −0.015], p = 0.047 (v2: −0.108, p = 0.016); M4 − M3 = +0.185, p = 0.008. The v2 reading stands on the current package: environment-aware aggregation beats pooled STABL and does not beat the simple meta-analysis ranking.
  • No candidate mechanism beat M0. M6 tied M0 on the ranking endpoint by construction (its ranking is the M0 ranking; its added value is the per-feature heterogeneity audit — 33 of 59 features BH-significant, 29 of those 33 failing Cochran’s Q at p < 0.10, median I² = 0.81 — and a strict native panel of 4 low-heterogeneity features, none in the source publication’s 20-population clock panel). M7 (0.219), M8 (0.109), and M9 (0.060) were all significantly worse than M0 (sign-flip p = 0.008). M7 ranked the paper’s GZMK+/GZMB+ Tem components #1 on the full atlas (top-20 panel concordance 0.85) but did not transport (LOCO 0.219): concordance without transportability.
  • ComBat-merge-then-select is an anti-pattern here. The failure is mechanistic: a label-free transform cannot reproduce the covariate terms of the training fit, so between-cohort outcome signal is removed before selection or prediction. Prediction MAE stays near the median baseline (18.5–18.9 years) even with a consistent transform (M9b), while every non-harmonized selector lands between 11.9 and 14.7.
  • Repositioned roles. The environment-stability workflow (M4/M5) is the transportability gate and batch-dependence diagnostic; per-cohort association with random-effects meta-analysis (M0, plus M6’s heterogeneity report) is the ranking workflow. Section 10.7’s conclusion is unchanged and now cross-validated on a pinned package with a wider method matrix.

Like this vignette, the v3 benchmark is a single application case study; it is not calibration evidence for any selector.
